questions.stem: An atom of carbon-14 has an atomic number of 6 and a mass number of 14. How many neutrons does it contain?
questions.explanation: Number of neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 14 - 6 = 8 neutrons. The mass number is the total of protons plus neutrons, and the atomic number is the number of protons. Option A gives the number of protons (not neutrons). Option C is the mass number itself. Option D adds them instead of subtracting.

questions.stem: In Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil. What did this observation demonstrate?

options.text: Alpha particles are too small to interact with gold atoms
Atoms are mostly empty space, with the mass concentrated in a tiny nucleus
Gold foil is not thick enough to stop alpha particles

questions.explanation: The fact that most alpha particles passed straight through showed that atoms are mostly empty space. The few that were deflected at large angles (or bounced back) showed that there is a small, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre. This disproved the 'plum pudding' model, which predicted that alpha particles would be slightly deflected but none would bounce back. Gold atoms do have nuclei (A). The observation is about atomic structure, not the size of alpha particles (B) or foil thickness (D).

questions.stem: An atom has 11 protons, 12 neutrons, and 11 electrons. If it loses one electron, what is the resulting particle?

options.text: A neutral atom with mass number 22
A positive ion with a charge of +1
A negative ion with a charge of -1
A different element with atomic number 10

questions.explanation: The atom starts with 11 protons (+11) and 11 electrons (-11), so it is neutral. Losing one electron gives it 11 protons and 10 electrons, resulting in a net charge of +1 -- a positive ion. The atomic number (number of protons) does not change, so it remains the same element (D is wrong). Losing an electron makes the charge positive, not negative (C is wrong).

questions.stem: The radius of an atom is approximately 1 x 10^-10 m. The radius of the nucleus is approximately 1 x 10^-14 m. How many times larger is the atom than the nucleus?
questions.explanation: Ratio = (1 x 10^-10) / (1 x 10^-14) = 10^(-10-(-14)) = 10^4 = 10,000. The atom is about 10,000 times larger than its nucleus. This enormous ratio explains why most of the atom is empty space, which is why most alpha particles pass straight through in scattering experiments. Options A, B, and C significantly underestimate how much bigger the atom is compared to the nucleus.

questions.stem: Isotopes of the same element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Which pair represents isotopes of the same element?

options.text: An atom with 6 protons and 6 neutrons, and an atom with 7 protons and 6 neutrons
An atom with 8 protons and 8 neutrons, and an atom with 8 protons and 10 neutrons
An atom with 6 protons and 6 neutrons, and an atom with 6 protons and 6 electrons
An atom with 12 protons and 12 neutrons, and an atom with 12 neutrons and 13 protons

questions.explanation: Isotopes must have the same number of protons (same element) but different numbers of neutrons. Option B has two atoms both with 8 protons (both oxygen) but different neutron numbers (8 and 10), making them oxygen-16 and oxygen-18 -- isotopes. Option A has different proton numbers (different elements). Option C describes the same atom (same protons and neutrons). Option D has different proton numbers (12 and 13), so they are different elements.
